subjects.title: CCAF 4 - Tools & MCP
subjects.description: Domain 4 (18%) - MCP architecture, primitives and transports, tool design, tool error handling, and MCP security.

cards.question: Your MCP server should expose a database schema that the model should always have available as background context. Which primitive?
cards.answer: A resource. Resources are application-controlled context data; tools are model-controlled actions. Running a query would be a tool; the schema itself is a resource.

choices.text: A resource
A tool
A prompt
A notification

hints: Is this something the model chooses to do, or something you hand it?

cards.question: The model keeps confusing two similar tools, `search` and `find`. What is the best fix?
cards.answer: This is an agent-computer-interface problem. Rename them to be specific and rewrite the descriptions to state when to use each versus the other. Adding examples to the system prompt patches a symptom of a bad tool contract. Merging them into one tool with an action parameter is also a documented pattern, but it is a bigger redesign than this naming bug needs.

choices.text: Rename them to specific, namespaced names and say when to use each
Add examples to the system prompt showing which of the two to pick
Add a keyword router that pre-selects the tool before each model turn
Reorder the tool list so the more frequently correct one is declared first

hints: This is an interface bug, not a prompt bug.

cards.question: A tool returns 4,000 database rows and the agent runs out of context two turns later. What is the best fix?
cards.answer: Fix it at the source: paginate and return only the fields the agent needs, with a total count and a cursor. Compaction and bigger models treat the symptom while the same flood happens on the next call. Lowering `max_tokens` limits what Claude writes, not what the tool returns.

choices.text: Paginate the tool, return only needed fields plus a total count and cursor
Summarize the conversation after each tool call so the rows get compressed
Move to a model whose context window can hold the full result set
Lower `max_tokens` so each model response is shorter and uses less context

hints: Fix it where the flood starts, not where it lands.

cards.question: Your team needs Claude Code to work with Jira issues. What is the recommended approach?
cards.answer: Choose existing community servers for standard integrations and reserve custom implementations for team-specific workflows. Project scope puts it in version control, so the whole team gets the same tooling.

choices.text: Use an existing community Jira MCP server, shared through the project's `.mcp.json` file
Build a custom Jira MCP server whose tool descriptions fit your team's vocabulary
Skip MCP and have Claude call the Jira REST API with curl
Add the Jira server to each developer's `~/.claude.json` so everyone controls their own

hints: Is issue tracking a standard integration or something only your team has?

cards.question: A research subagent only needs to read. Which tool exposure is correct?
cards.answer: Least privilege: expose only the read tools it needs. Every extra tool costs context on every request, raises mis-selection, and widens the blast radius.

choices.text: Expose only the read tools it needs and deny the write servers
Expose everything and rely on the system prompt to say it is read-only
Expose everything so it never gets blocked mid-task
Expose everything but set temperature to 0

hints: Least privilege - and remember every extra tool also costs context.

cards.question: Two tools, `analyze_content` and `analyze_document`, have near-identical descriptions and the agent keeps misrouting between them. What is the fix?
cards.answer: Ambiguous or overlapping descriptions cause misrouting, and the named fix is renaming plus a description that eliminates the functional overlap - `analyze_content` becomes `extract_web_results` with a web-specific description. Tool order and system prompt patches leave the two descriptions as confusing as before.

choices.text: Rename one to reflect its actual domain and rewrite its description around that
Reorder the tools so the one needed more often is listed first
Add a system prompt paragraph explaining which tool to use in which situation
Remove one of them and let the remaining tool handle both kinds of input

hints: The tools do different things. Only their labels say otherwise.

cards.question: Tool descriptions are careful and distinct, but the agent still over-uses the search tool. What should you inspect?
cards.answer: System prompt wording affects tool selection: an instruction like "always look for the latest information" pulls toward the search tool regardless of how well the other descriptions are written. Reviewing the system prompt for those accidental associations is the named skill.

choices.text: The system prompt, for keyword-sensitive wording that creates unintended tool associations
The tool schemas, for optional parameters that make search the cheapest call
The tool ordering, since tools listed first get selected more often
The conversation history, for earlier turns where search returned useful results

hints: Something outside the tool definitions is competing with them.

cards.question: A refund request falls outside the return window. What should `process_refund` return?
cards.answer: A policy violation is a business error: retrying will never succeed, so `retriable: false` stops the loop, and the customer-friendly explanation gives the agent something accurate to say instead of improvising a reason.

choices.text: A business error marked `retriable: false`, with an explanation the customer can understand
A transient error, so the agent retries in case the window changed
A validation error, since the date argument fell outside the accepted range
A successful response with a zero refund amount and an empty reason field

hints: Nothing about retrying this will change the answer.

cards.question: A search subagent's query runs successfully and matches nothing. How should that be reported?
cards.answer: The guide separates access failures - which need a retry decision - from valid empty results, which are successful queries with no matches. Reporting an empty result as a failure triggers pointless retries; reporting a failure as empty makes the report claim nothing exists.

choices.text: As a successful result that is empty, distinct from any access failure
As a transient error, so the coordinator retries the query against another source
As a validation error, since the query as written produced no usable output
As a silent no-op, letting the coordinator infer the gap from the missing section

hints: Nothing went wrong. That is the whole point.

cards.question: A subagent hits a transient timeout on one of its sources. What should it do before telling the coordinator?
cards.answer: Subagents implement local recovery for transient failures and propagate only what they cannot resolve - along with partial results and what was attempted. Routing every hiccup to the coordinator wastes the hub's attention; returning partial work as success hides the gap.

choices.text: Attempt local recovery, and propagate only if it cannot resolve the failure itself
Propagate immediately, since the coordinator owns all error handling in hub-and-spoke
Retry indefinitely with backoff, because a transient failure resolves on its own
Return its partial results as a success, so the coordinator's synthesis is not blocked

hints: The coordinator should hear about what could not be fixed, not about everything.

cards.question: The synthesis subagent has been given the web-search tool for convenience, and it now runs searches instead of synthesizing. What is the principle being violated?
cards.answer: Agents with tools outside their specialization tend to misuse them - this exact example is named. The fix is restricting each subagent's tool set to its role, with a narrow cross-role tool like `verify_fact` where the need is genuinely frequent.

choices.text: Scoped tool access - agents misuse tools that fall outside their specialization
Tool count limits - every extra tool makes selection less reliable overall
Context isolation - search results flood a window meant for findings only
Hub-and-spoke routing - the subagent now reaches around the coordinator

hints: It is not doing anything forbidden. It is doing someone else's job.

cards.question: Document type is unknown and several extraction schemas exist. You need a tool call rather than prose. Which `tool_choice`?
cards.answer: `"any"` guarantees the model calls a tool while leaving the choice open, which is exactly the case where the document type is unknown. `"auto"` permits a text answer; forcing one specific tool defeats the purpose when you cannot know which schema applies. Note: on Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, `"any"` and forced `tool` return a 400; there you use `"auto"` with strict tool use or structured outputs.

choices.text: `"any"`, which forces a tool call but lets the model choose which
`"auto"`, which lets the model call a tool or reply in text
Forced selection, naming the extraction tool that fits most document types
`"auto"` plus a prompt line instructing the model never to answer in prose

hints: You know a call must happen, but not which schema fits.

cards.question: An agent needs to load documents, but its `fetch_url` tool will retrieve anything on the web. What is the recommended change?
cards.answer: Replacing a generic tool with a constrained alternative is the named skill - the restriction lives in the tool, so misuse becomes impossible rather than discouraged. A prompt rule is a request; post-hoc validation happens after the fetch already occurred.

choices.text: Replace it with a `load_document` tool that only accepts validated document URLs
Keep `fetch_url` and add a system prompt rule limiting it to documents
Keep `fetch_url` and validate the retrieved content type after the call returns
Remove `fetch_url` and route every document load through the coordinator instead

hints: Make the wrong call impossible rather than asking for it not to happen.

cards.question: A shared MCP server needs a `GITHUB_TOKEN` and the config must be committed. How?
cards.answer: Environment variable expansion in `.mcp.json` is the named mechanism for credential management without committing secrets. Personal config would keep the secret out of git but loses the shared team tooling that project scope exists to provide, and `.claude/settings.json` is committed too.

choices.text: Project `.mcp.json` with `${GITHUB_TOKEN}` expanded from each developer's own environment
Project `.mcp.json` with the token value, since the repository is private
Personal `~/.claude.json` per developer, each holding that developer's own token
Project `.claude/settings.json` holding the token, since settings never reach the model

hints: The config is shared. The secret is not.

cards.question: Your MCP server exposes a powerful code-search tool, but the agent keeps using the built-in `Grep` instead. What is the fix?
cards.answer: A thin description loses tool selection to a familiar built-in. Enhancing it to explain capabilities and outputs is the named fix. Removing `Grep` might force the behavior, but it strips a genuinely useful tool to make up for documentation you could just write. Note: on macOS, Linux and WSL, current Claude Code leaves Grep out of the default tool set and searches with `grep` through Bash; the fix is the same.

choices.text: Enhance the MCP tool description to explain its capabilities and outputs in detail
Remove `Grep` from the agent's allowed tools so only the MCP tool remains
Rename the MCP tool to match words the prompt already uses
Move the server from user scope to project scope so it loads first

hints: The built-in is not better. It is better explained.

cards.question: The agent needs every test file in the repository, wherever it sits. Which built-in tool is meant for this?
cards.answer: Glob is for file path pattern matching - finding files by name or extension. Grep searches contents, which would also match files that merely mention the test library, and Read loads file contents, not file lists. Note: on macOS, Linux and WSL, current Claude Code leaves Glob and Grep out of the default tool set and runs `find` and `grep` through Bash instead; the exam key is Glob.

choices.text: `Glob`, matching file paths against a pattern like `**/*.test.tsx`
`Grep`, searching file contents for imports of the testing library
`Read`, opening the test runner config to list its files
`Read`, loading each directory listing and filtering the names

hints: You know the shape of the filename, not what is inside it.

cards.question: An agent must understand an unfamiliar service before changing it. What is the recommended approach?
cards.answer: Building codebase understanding incrementally is the named skill: start with Grep to find entry points, then Read to follow imports and trace flows, rather than reading everything upfront and exhausting the context on material you did not need. Note: on macOS, Linux and WSL, current Claude Code runs content search as `grep` through Bash instead of a separate Grep tool; the incremental approach is the same.

choices.text: Grep for entry points, then Read to follow imports and trace the flows
Read every file in the service directory so nothing important is missed early
Glob the directory tree first, then Read the files with the largest line counts
Ask Bash for a dependency graph, then Read only the most depended-upon modules

hints: Reading everything is thorough and is still the wrong answer.

cards.question: Your document store MCP tool returns the same isError response whether the file is missing, the format is unsupported, or the storage service timed out. The agent retries all three the same number of times. What should the tool return instead?
cards.answer: Distinct error categories carrying a retryable flag let the agent retry the timeout and stop retrying the unsupported format, which is what prevents wasted retries on permanent failures. The raw storage exception leaks internals and still leaves the retry decision ambiguous. One error type with a suggested wait assumes everything is transient. An empty document reports a failure as a success.

choices.text: Distinct categories with an isRetryable flag, so a timeout is retried and an unsupported format is not.
The underlying storage exception verbatim, giving the agent the most detailed possible information.
A single error type with a suggested wait time, since retries are the only recovery path available.
A successful response containing an empty document, so the agent can continue with the remaining files.

hints: The agent needs to know whether trying again could ever work.

cards.question: You added an MCP server that exposes rich, indexed code search over your monorepo, but the agent keeps using the built-in Grep tool and gets worse results. The MCP tool is registered and its description reads "Searches code". What should you do first?
cards.answer: An agent falls back to the built-in tool when an MCP tool's description does not communicate what it adds, so the first move is to say what it indexes, what it returns, and when it beats plain text search. Removing Grep takes away a tool that is genuinely right for some queries. Renaming for list position treats ordering as relevance. A blanket CLAUDE.md prohibition misfires on the cases where Grep is the correct choice.

choices.text: Expand the MCP tool's description to explain what it indexes, what it returns, and when it beats plain text search.
Remove Grep from the agent's allowed tools in this repository so the MCP tool becomes the only code search option available.
Rename the MCP tool to something that sorts before Grep in the tool list the model receives.
Add an instruction in CLAUDE.md telling the agent never to use Grep in this repository.

hints: The model can only prefer what the description tells it about.

cards.question: An engineer asks the agent to find every place a deprecated function named calculateTax is called, and separately to list every Storybook story file in the repository. Which tools should the agent use for each task?
cards.answer: Grep searches file **contents** for a pattern, which is how you find every caller of `calculateTax`; Glob matches file **paths** by name or extension, which is how you list the story files. Doing it the other way round misuses each tool. Grep for both turns a path question into a content search. Reading every file exhausts the context window for an answer two tool calls would give.

choices.text: Grep for the calculateTax callers, Glob for the story files.
Glob for the calculateTax callers, Grep for the story files.
Grep for both, since it can match file names as well as file contents.
Read every file in the repository once and answer both questions from what it loaded.

hints: One question is about what is inside files, the other about what the files are called.

cards.question: Your team wants the agent to read and comment on Jira issues. A maintained community MCP server for Jira already exists and covers your use cases. An engineer proposes writing your own server instead. How should you decide?
cards.answer: A maintained community server is the recommended choice for a standard integration, leaving custom servers for workflows that are specific to your team. Building your own for a solved problem pays a maintenance cost for nothing. Forking on day one takes on that maintenance with no stated need. The claim that community servers cannot expand environment variables for credentials is simply not true.

choices.text: Adopt the community server for the standard integration, and build custom servers only for team-specific workflows.
Build the custom server, since owning the code makes debugging and future changes easier.
Build the custom server, because community MCP servers cannot use environment variable expansion for authentication credentials.
Adopt the community server and immediately fork it so the team controls its release schedule.

hints: Custom work is for what nobody else can provide.

cards.question: Your boilerplate generator must always call extract_project_metadata before any of the code generation tools, so the generated files match the project's conventions. Which configuration guarantees the first call?
cards.answer: `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_project_metadata"}` names the tool the model must call, which is the only option that guarantees which call comes first; later turns can go back to `auto`. `tool_choice: "any"` forces a tool call but not which one. `auto` plus ordering described in the descriptions leaves it to the model's judgment. Position in the `tools` array is not a constraint.

choices.text: Force the first call with tool_choice set to that specific tool, then continue normally in follow-up turns.
Set tool_choice to "any" so the model is required to call a tool on the first turn.
Set tool_choice to "auto" and describe the required ordering in the tool descriptions.
List extract_project_metadata first in the tools array so the model encounters it before the others.

hints: One setting names the tool; the others only say that some tool must be called.

cards.question: The agent tries to update a validation block in a large file, but Edit fails because the anchor text it chose appears four times. It has already retried with slightly longer anchors and failed again. What is the reliable fallback?
cards.answer: When Edit cannot find unique anchor text, Read the full file and Write it back with the change applied - that is the documented fallback for a reliable modification. A `sed` replacement of the fourth occurrence is brittle and easy to get wrong on offsets. Splitting the file is a refactor motivated by a tooling limitation. Editing all four and reverting three deliberately introduces three defects.

choices.text: Read the full file, then Write it back with the modification applied.
Run a Bash sed command that replaces only the fourth occurrence by line number.
Split the file into smaller modules first so the anchor becomes unique.
Apply the edit to all four occurrences and then revert the three unintended ones.

hints: The documented fallback replaces the whole file instead of hunting for a unique anchor.
